b.x: This does not teach breaking into a house, trapping the ground, or sleeping with a coal inside the tarp. Charcoal or fire in a closed car kills by carbon monoxide. Flood: do not stop at the bottom of the valley. This page does not dial.

While the house is standing and the water is not rising, you do not leave to build. Close one door. Choose one room only. The cold floor steals heat: a mattress, clean cardboard, or a blanket under the body, not only on top. Window closed to the wind, open enough for air if the room gets stuffy. Candle away from the curtain. One light only. A mosquito net, if the house has one, because in Brazil the mosquito sickens you before the film's cold. Trash out of the room. The whole family in the same room warms more than four open doors. That is shelter. The park, at night, with two children, is not.
When the house will not do

Flood on the floor, fire, a roof about to fall: you leave. The destination is what is on the paper, by day, the four together, with the bag that looks like travel. It is not a tarp in the square. A tarp in the square says you have what the others do not. The gray man does not pitch a camp in sight. If night caught you on the way and there is no door, then yes, the shelter of one night. It is not a new house. It is not sleeping in the rain.

Look for an hour, not a minute. Out of a dry riverbed: the rain at dawn fills it without warning. Out from under a dead branch. Off the path, so nobody trips over you in the dark. A little high, so the water runs down. Near fine wood only if you are going to light, and the fire stays outside the tarp, as on the fire page. In the brush, ground without an anthill and without an animal trail. In the city, a recess in a wall is still the street: you are visible. If a relative's door is two hours of walking and there is still light in the sky, walk. Do not build.

One tarp, a thick plastic sheet, or a clean rubble bag with no chemical. One rope at chest height, between two trees or two firm points, away from the street. The tarp over the rope, both sides down to the ground, held with stone, not with the pack: the pack stays with you. The floor inside gets what insulates: cardboard, dry leaf, clothes that are not on the body. The body does not lie on bare earth. The opening faces away from the wind and stays small. It fits the family, shoulder to shoulder. It does not fit a campfire. The rain runs off the outside. If the plastic touches the skin all night, the skin gets wet from its own sweat. Leave a gap. In the morning, take it down. A one-night shelter that stays by day becomes an address.

If there is no plastic, the shelter is bulk. A fallen trunk or a low wall makes the wind's wall. On the protected side, a mattress of leaves, dry grass, or cardboard, thicker than your open hand. On the body, whatever is dry, and the children between the adults. It is not a handbook hut. It is not giving your heat to the ground and the wind until morning. Wet on top and wet underneath, the night drops people in weather that by day did not seem cold. If you found a door before that, the leaves stay in the brush.
